tagline.text: A limestone archipelago of giant legends and a scallop feast

children.text: A cluster of a dozen or so islands scattered in the waters off Carles, at the northeastern tip of Panay Island. This hidden hopping destination in West Visayas is known for emerald lagoons between limestone cliffs, white sandbars, and a near-endless feast of scallops.

Islas de Gigantes means "Islands of the Giants" in Spanish. It's a cluster of a dozen or so islands scattered in the Visayan Sea off the municipality of Carles, at the northeastern tip of Panay Island; most residents live on the two largest islands, Gigantes Norte and Gigantes Sur, while the rest are small uninhabited islets and rock formations. The name is said to come from an old legend that oversized coffins and bones, believed to belong to giants, were found in caves on the islands.

The scenery here recalls El Nido or Coron — limestone cliffs and jagged rock formations rising from the sea, white sand beaches hidden among them, sandbars exposed at low tide, and emerald lagoons formed where seawater seeps through cracks in the rock. Yet because it's inconvenient to reach, the islands stayed largely unknown to foreign travellers for a long time, leaving behind a relatively cheap and unpolished atmosphere.

Gigantes is also known as the island of scallops. So many scallops are caught in the surrounding waters that there was once a saying that a single scallop cost only one or two pesos. Even today, hopping tour lunches come piled high with scallops, crab, squid, and shellfish dishes, earning it the nickname "the all-you-can-eat scallop feast."
In

, the massive typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) struck this area and caused heavy damage, but residents rebuilt the community around tourism. Facilities are still basic, so it suits adventurous travellers who enjoy village homestays, beach camping, seafood, and hopping tours more than upscale resorts.
A narrow strip of sand connecting two rocky hills creates Gigantes' iconic scenery. Climb a short rocky path to the viewpoint, and the sea unfolds on both sides in a single sweeping view.

A natural saltwater pool enclosed by limestone cliffs on Gigantes Sur island. Seawater flows in and out through cracks in the rock, giving the water an emerald color, and whether you can enter depends on the tide.
A small stretch of white sand hidden beneath towering rock cliffs, a good spot for swimming and snorkeling during a hopping tour.
A long white sandbar that emerges at low tide, letting you take photos that look like you're walking in the middle of the sea.
A stop for snorkeling in the clear water around this small island, followed by rest on the beach.
Feast on steamed or grilled scallops, crab, squid, and shellfish dishes served as the joiner tour lunch. You can also buy extra scallops at local prices and have them cooked for you.
The ruins of a Spanish-era lighthouse on a hill at the north of the island; a short trek rewards you with a sweeping view of the Visayan Sea.

and may vary depending on local conditions.
Most accommodation is in homestays and small resorts in the villages of Gigantes Norte and Gigantes Sur. Fan rooms cost around
a night, while air-conditioned rooms or beach cottages run about

. Beach camping is possible on some islands. Electricity is sometimes limited to certain hours, so check the air conditioning and generator schedule when booking. There are also small accommodations on the Carles mainland near Bancal Port, handy for a late arrival.

Seafood is, without question, the star of the food here. Scallops grilled or steamed with butter and garlic, crab, grilled squid, fish kinilaw, and shellfish soup all appear at tour lunches and at your accommodation. Scallops can be bought cheaply on the spot by weight or count, and many travellers arrange a seafood party through their accommodation. There are no convenience stores on the islands, so buy snacks, drinks, and any food you prefer beforehand in Carles.
There are no ATMs on the islands. Since transport, accommodation, tours, and entrance fees must all be paid in cash, withdraw plenty in Iloilo or Roxas beforehand.
Phone signal is unreliable and varies by island and location. Save your accommodation's and tour operator's contact details in advance.
Missing the early morning bus from Iloilo makes it hard to catch the public boat that day. Check the first departure time and leave with plenty of margin.
The rocky paths to the Cabugao Gamay viewpoint and the lighthouse are slippery and sharp. Wear aqua shoes or sandal-style trekking shoes.
There's a lot of spray during bangka rides, so a waterproof pouch or dry bag is essential.
If you're planning to eat a lot of scallops, check for seafood allergies beforehand and bring your own medication.
A
1-night, 2-day
package handles transport connections and the hopping order for you, making it especially convenient for first-time visitors.

On many parts of the island, electricity comes on only for a few hours from dusk into the night and early morning. Bring a fully charged power bank, and Smart tends to have relatively better mobile signal.
On days with high waves, the coast guard can suspend boat service. Don't push for a departure and build a spare day into your schedule.
Tangke Lagoon is enclosed by cliffs and narrow rock gaps, which can be dangerous at high tide or in rough seas. Follow your guide's judgment, and only cliff-dive after confirming the water depth.
Don't touch marine life or coral, or collect shells or coral fragments. Always carry your trash out with you.
Freshness is everything with seafood. Avoid food that's been left out too long, and don't overdo it on raw dishes.
Entrance fees, environmental charges, and boat schedules change often under the Carles municipal government's policies, so check the latest notice.
Always wear a life jacket while travelling between islands. Small bangkas roll easily in rough water, and the nearest hospital is on the mainland.
